wrongOptionNotes.C: Terminating instances reactively after they are launched causes service disruption; proactive prevention via SCPs is much more effective.

questions.question: An e-commerce platform experiences sudden traffic surges during flash sales. The application tier consists of stateless EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The engineering team notices that when Auto Scaling launches new instances, it takes several minutes before they can successfully handle traffic due to application startup initialization.

options.text: Increase the health check grace period on the Application Load Balancer target group to a higher threshold.
Configure a scheduled scaling action to scale up the Auto Scaling group 2 hours before every flash sale.
Configure an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling lifecycle hook to put newly launched instances into a Pending:Wait state until initialization scripts complete, and implement warm pools.
Migrate the application from EC2 instances to Amazon S3 static website hosting combined with Amazon CloudFront.

questions.explanation: To minimize cold-start latency during dynamic scaling events, Auto Scaling lifecycle hooks pause instance registration until setup completes, and warm pools keep pre-warmed instances ready for instant deployment.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While a grace period prevents premature health check failures, it does not keep instances in a pre-initialized ready state or accelerate cold-start times like warm pools.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Scheduled scaling helps with predictable traffic, but flash sales can occur unexpectedly or vary in intensity, making dynamic scaling with warm pools necessary.
wrongOptionNotes.D: An e-commerce application with dynamic backend logic cannot be hosted purely as a static website on S3 and CloudFront.

questions.question: A financial company needs to design a disaster recovery (DR) strategy for a core PostgreSQL database currently running on Amazon RDS. The business requirement states that the Recovery Point Objective (RPO) must be less than 5 seconds, and the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) must be less than 1 minute across regions.

options.text: Take daily snapshots of the Amazon RDS database and copy the snapshot to the target DR region every 24 hours.
Deploy a separate independent RDS instance in the DR region and write a custom application script to dual-write all transactions from the application layer to both databases.
Set up a scheduled AWS Backup plan to replicate database backups to an S3 bucket in another AWS Region every hour.
Configure an Amazon RDS Cross-Region Read Replica in the target DR region, ensuring synchronous or near-synchronous replication is active.

questions.explanation: Amazon RDS Cross-Region Read Replicas provide an efficient way to achieve low RPO and RTO for disaster recovery by asynchronously replicating data to another region and allowing quick promotion.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Daily snapshots result in an RPO of 24 hours and a high RTO due to the time required to restore a database from a snapshot, failing both requirements.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Dual-writing from the application layer is prone to data inconsistency, split-brain scenarios, and high operational complexity compared to native RDS replication.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Hourly backups yield an RPO of 1 hour, which fails the strict requirement of an RPO under 5 seconds.

questions.question: A gaming company hosts a multiplayer game backend on AWS. The architecture uses Amazon DynamoDB tables for storing player profiles and game state data. During global tournaments, the database experiences read throttling due to hot keys where millions of players access the same leaderboard data simultaneously.

options.text: Migrate the DynamoDB tables from provisioned capacity mode to on-demand capacity mode.
Enable Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) in front of the DynamoDB tables to cache read-heavy queries and reduce latency.
Increase the read capacity units (RCUs) on the DynamoDB table using target tracking auto scaling.
Convert the DynamoDB table into a global table with replicas in every AWS Region.

questions.explanation: Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache that sits in front of DynamoDB tables, absorbing read traffic spikes and hot keys to protect the database from throttling.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While on-demand mode handles unpredictable workloads, hot-key throttling on a single partition is still subject to partition-level limits, making caching via DAX necessary.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Scaling total table RCUs does not solve hot-key issues because DynamoDB partitions data by primary key, and a single partition still has strict throughput limits.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Global tables improve latency and availability across regions, but they do not solve the hot-key partition limitation for identical queries hitting the same item.

questions.question: An enterprise is planning to migrate 50 TB of on-premises NAS file storage to Amazon S3. The data transfer must be completed within 2 weeks, but the company's internet connection is limited to 100 Mbps, which is insufficient for transferring the volume over the public internet in the required timeframe.

options.text: Order an AWS Snowball Edge Storage Optimized device to copy the data locally and ship it back to AWS for import into Amazon S3.
Provision an AWS Direct Connect dedicated 1 Gbps connection to transfer the files directly over a private link.
Set up an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection over the existing 100 Mbps internet link and stream the data continuously.
Use AWS DataSync with multiple parallel streams over the public internet to saturate the 100 Mbps bandwidth.

questions.explanation: When network bandwidth is inadequate to transfer massive datasets within required timelines, physical migration devices like AWS Snowball Edge provide a secure, high-speed offline data transfer mechanism.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Provisioning and installing a dedicated Direct Connect circuit typically takes weeks or months, missing the immediate migration deadline.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Transferring 50 TB over a 100 Mbps connection takes over 40 days theoretically, which violates the 2-week deadline.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Even with optimal parallel streams, the physical limit of a 100 Mbps line makes transferring 50 TB within 2 weeks mathematically impossible.

questions.question: A financial analytics company stores sensitive customer data in an Amazon S3 bucket. Compliance standards require that all objects uploaded to the bucket must be encrypted using customer-managed encryption keys, and any objects uploaded with unapproved encryption methods must be automatically rejected.

options.text: Configure an AWS CloudTrail log analyzer to alert the security team whenever an unencrypted object is detected in the bucket.
Apply an Amazon S3 bucket policy with a condition denying requests where s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption does not equal aws:kms or uses an unauthorized KMS key ARN.
Set up an AWS Lambda function triggered by S3 Event Notifications to re-encrypt any unencrypted files uploaded to the bucket.
Enable default encryption on the S3 bucket using Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3).

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 bucket policies with conditional statements allow you to enforce strict server-side encryption standards, ensuring that unauthorized upload requests are rejected at the API level.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Alerting is reactive and does not prevent the upload of unencrypted data as required by the compliance mandate.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Re-encrypting files after upload leaves a window of vulnerability where unencrypted data briefly exists in the bucket, violating strict compliance guardrails.
wrongOptionNotes.D: SSE-S3 uses AWS-managed keys rather than customer-managed keys, failing the compliance requirement for customer-managed keys.

questions.question: A media publishing company hosts a dynamic news website on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The site experiences unpredictable traffic spikes. The architecture needs to reduce database load and improve response times for static content assets.

options.text: Deploy an Amazon ElastiCache for Redis cluster to store backend session state data.
Create multiple read replicas of the backend database and configure application-level round-robin routing.
Place Amazon CloudFront in front of the Application Load Balancer to cache static and dynamic content at edge locations globally.
Migrate all backend EC2 instances to larger instance sizes with more CPU and RAM.

questions.explanation: Integrating Amazon CloudFront with an Application Load Balancer offloads static and cacheable dynamic content to edge servers, improving performance and protecting origin servers.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While ElastiCache helps with session state, it does not cache static web assets or provide global content delivery like CloudFront.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Database read replicas do not cache web assets or reduce HTTP request load on the web servers.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Vertical scaling is expensive and does not solve network latency or cache static content efficiently at the network edge.

questions.question: A company is designing a multi-tier web application in AWS. The architecture includes public subnets for an Application Load Balancer and private subnets for application EC2 instances and an Amazon RDS database. Security mandates that the database instances must never be accessible from the public internet, even via a bastion host.

options.text: Configure an AWS Network Firewall to inspect all traffic leaving the database subnet towards the internet.
Place the database instances in public subnets but assign them a restrictive security group that blocks all inbound ports except port 3306 from the application servers.
Place the database instances in isolated private subnets with no route to an Internet Gateway or NAT Gateway, and restrict security groups to allow traffic only from the application EC2 instances.
Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the database subnet to filter out malicious public traffic.

questions.explanation: Secure multi-tier architectures place databases in private subnets with no internet gateway or NAT gateway routes, relying strictly on internal VPC security groups for tier-to-tier communication.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Databases in private application tiers should not have any routing path to the internet in the first place, rendering firewalls redundant for internet isolation.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Placing database instances in public subnets exposes them to potential IP scanning and misconfiguration risks, violating best security practices.
wrongOptionNotes.D: AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks on ELBs, CloudFront, and Route 53, but it does not fix architectural misplacement of databases in public subnets.

questions.question: An enterprise application requires centralized secret management for database credentials, API keys, and OAuth tokens. The credentials must be automatically rotated every 30 days without requiring application downtime.

options.text: Encrypt the secrets using AWS KMS and store them in an Amazon S3 bucket, using a scheduled CloudWatch event to update the files.
Store the credentials in AWS Secrets Manager and configure its built-in automated rotation feature using AWS Lambda.
Store the credentials as plaintext environment variables in the Amazon ECS task definitions.
Store the credentials in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store with standard tier configuration.

questions.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager is designed specifically for rotating, managing, and retrieving database credentials and API keys securely with native Lambda rotation support.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Building a custom rotation mechanism around S3 and KMS introduces unnecessary maintenance overhead and reinvents built-in features provided by Secrets Manager.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Storing credentials in plain text environment variables is a severe security risk and does not support automated rotation.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Parameter Store is great for configuration data and secure strings, it lacks the native automated rotation workflows built into AWS Secrets Manager.

questions.question: A global SaaS application deployed on AWS uses Amazon Route 53 as its DNS service. The architecture requires high availability and intelligent routing to direct users to the lowest-latency AWS Region, while automatically failing over to a secondary region if the primary region experiences an outage.

options.text: Configure Route 53 latency routing policies combined with Route 53 health checks to monitor endpoints and automatically route traffic away from unhealthy regions.
Configure Route 53 geoproximity routing to route traffic based on the geographic location of users and resources.
Use Route 53 simple routing policy with a weighted round-robin distribution across regions.
Deploy an Amazon CloudFront distribution with multiple origin groups configured for failover.

questions.explanation: Amazon Route 53 latency routing combined with health checks provides optimal multi-region performance and automated resilience by routing users to the fastest available endpoint.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Geoproximity routing routes traffic based on geographic coordinates and bias parameters rather than real-time network latency measurements.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Simple routing does not factor in user latency or perform health check failovers between regions.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While CloudFront handles edge caching and origin failover, Route 53 latency routing operates at the DNS level for multi-region backend routing.

questions.question: A financial company needs to collect real-time stock ticker data from thousands of feeds, process the data stream with minimal latency, and store the aggregated results into an Amazon S3 data lake for compliance auditing.

options.text: Configure an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database to accept direct inserts from all feeds and run scheduled database triggers.
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for real-time ingestion, AWS Lambda for stream processing, and Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to deliver data into Amazon S3.
Set up an Amazon SQS standard queue to receive feeds, and poll the queue using an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances.
Write incoming stock feeds to an Amazon S3 bucket every minute using client scripts, and run an AWS Glue job hourly to process the files.

questions.explanation: For real-time streaming analytics and reliable delivery to data lakes, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams combined with Lambda and Kinesis Data Firehose offers a scalable, low-latency architecture.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Relational databases will quickly experience write bottlenecks and high costs when ingesting thousands of high-frequency real-time financial feeds.
wrongOptionNotes.C: SQS is a message queue designed for decoupling task processing, whereas Kinesis is built for high-throughput real-time streaming data pipelines.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Batch processing data hourly introduces high latency and does not meet the requirement for real-time streaming and processing.

questions.question: A global media company is designing an image-processing service that receives high volumes of unpredictable image upload requests. The architecture uses Amazon EC2 instances managed by an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer to process the images and store them in Amazon S3. During peak hours, the EC2 instances experience high CPU utilization, causing significant processing delays because the Auto Scaling group takes several minutes to launch new instances. How should a solutions architect redesign this architecture to improve performance and responsiveness during traffic spikes?

options.text: Migrate the application workload to AWS Lambda and configure Amazon S3 event notifications to trigger the function directly for each uploaded image.
Increase the maximum size of the EC2 Auto Scaling group and configure predictive scaling based on historical machine learning patterns.
Place an Amazon SQS queue in front of the EC2 Auto Scaling group and scale the instances based on the ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible metric.
Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Network Load Balancer and use larger EC2 instance types to handle more concurrent processing threads.

questions.explanation: For unpredictable, bursty workloads, serverless architectures like AWS Lambda provide optimal performance and responsiveness. Lambda automatically scales execution environments concurrently in milliseconds to handle incoming requests without the cold-start and provisioning delays associated with Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Predictive scaling helps with predictable, recurring traffic patterns, but it cannot instantly react to sudden, unpredictable spikes in real-time image uploads.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While SQS decouples the intake from processing, it still relies on EC2 Auto Scaling, which suffers from instance startup latency during sudden spikes compared to serverless execution.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Larger instances do not solve the fundamental scaling delay issue of Auto Scaling groups during sudden traffic surges, and NLB is unnecessary for HTTP/HTTPS workloads.

questions.question: A company runs a batch-processing application on Amazon EC2 instances managed by an Auto Scaling group. The workload runs every night for four hours and can be interrupted without data loss if it is resumed or restarted. The architecture must minimize operational overhead while reducing EC2 costs as much as possible.

options.text: Use Reserved Instances matching the instance family and size used by the batch processing application.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances with a mixed instances policy and capacity-optimized allocation strategy.
Implement an AWS Lambda function to provision and terminate On-Demand EC2 instances using a cron schedule via Amazon EventBridge.
Purchase Compute Savings Plans to cover the baseline capacity needed for the nightly batch window.

questions.explanation: For fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads, Amazon EC2 Spot Instances offer the highest cost savings. Using an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy and the capacity-optimized strategy ensures high availability while minimizing the risk of interruption and operational overhead.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Reserved Instances commit to instances running 24/7 or significant portions of a month, which is inefficient for a workload that only runs four hours a night.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While this automates scheduling, On-Demand instances are far more expensive than Spot Instances, and managing custom scripts adds unnecessary operational overhead compared to Auto Scaling.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Savings Plans provide a discount for commitment, but Spot Instances provide significantly higher savings (up to 90%) for workloads that can tolerate interruptions.

questions.question: An enterprise web application stores user-uploaded documents in an Amazon S3 bucket. Over the past year, millions of files have accumulated. Approximately 80% of these files are accessed frequently for the first 30 days, rarely accessed between 30 and 90 days, and virtually never accessed after 90 days, though they must be retained for compliance for 7 years. Which solution provides the most cost-effective storage architecture?

options.text: Configure an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days, and to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days.
Transition all objects directly to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately upon upload using an S3 Event Notification triggering an AWS Lambda function.
Keep all objects in S3 Standard and use Amazon CloudFront to cache the documents at edge locations.
Configure an S3 Lifecycle rule to transition objects to Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering immediately upon upload.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies automate moving data to cheaper storage tiers based on age. S3 Standard-IA is cost-effective for data accessed infrequently after 30 days, and S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval provides the lowest cost for long-term compliance storage.

wrongOptionNotes.B: The data is accessed frequently for the first 30 days. S3 Glacier Deep Archive has retrieval fees and minimum storage duration charges that would make frequent access during the first month cost-prohibitive.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CloudFront caches frequently accessed data at the edge, but it does not reduce the underlying storage cost of millions of objects sitting in S3 Standard storage.
wrongOptionNotes.D: S3 Intelligent-Tiering has a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object, making it less cost-effective for large quantities of objects that have predictable, long-term lifecycle access patterns compared to standard S3 Lifecycle rules.

questions.question: A solutions architect is designing a multi-tier web application running on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application experiences predictable daily traffic peaks during business hours and very low traffic at night. The database runs on Amazon RDS. The company wants to optimize infrastructure costs during off-peak hours.

options.text: Use AWS Auto Scaling to scale out the EC2 instances during business hours and scale them in at night, and stop the RDS database instance during off-peak hours.
Configure an Auto Scaling scheduled scaling policy to adjust the desired capacity of EC2 instances based on traffic patterns, and purchase EC2 Savings Plans for baseline capacity.
Use Amazon CloudFront in front of the ALB to cache all dynamic responses, allowing the EC2 Auto Scaling group to scale down to zero instances at night.
Migrate the entire application architecture to AWS Lambda and Amazon DynamoDB on-demand capacity.

questions.explanation: Predictable traffic spikes are best managed using scheduled Auto Scaling policies combined with Savings Plans for baseline compute. Databases generally need to remain running to maintain connection states and backend operations unless specific serverless architectures are adopted.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Amazon RDS instances cannot be simply 'stopped' for more than 7 days without automatically restarting, and stopping a primary database entirely breaks the web application connectivity unless it is read-only traffic.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CloudFront cannot cache dynamic responses effectively without complex customization, and Auto Scaling groups cannot scale EC2 instances behind an ALB safely to zero while maintaining target group attachments.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Rewriting a traditional multi-tier EC2/RDS application to serverless introduces significant development and refactoring effort, violating the requirement for minimal operational/refactoring overhead.

questions.question: A company is running an analytics platform on Amazon EMR clusters that process large datasets stored in Amazon S3. The jobs run intermittently throughout the week. Currently, the EMR clusters are launched using On-Demand instances, resulting in high monthly costs. The analytics jobs can tolerate cluster termination if instance capacity becomes unavailable.

options.text: Migrate all EMR nodes to Dedicated Hosts to secure maximum volume discounts.
Purchase Amazon EMR Reserved Instances for the maximum possible cluster size.
Modify the EMR cluster configuration to use a combination of On-Demand instances for the master node and Spot instances for core and task nodes.
Convert the EMR cluster into a single monolithic Amazon EC2 instance running Hadoop.

questions.explanation: Amazon EMR natively supports instance fleets and instance groups configured with Spot instances. Utilizing Spot instances for task and core nodes minimizes cost for fault-tolerant batch analytics jobs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive EC2 pricing model, designed for compliance and license-bring-your-own requirements, not cost optimization.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Because the jobs run intermittently throughout the week rather than continuously, purchasing Reserved Instances for peak capacity leads to wasted idle capacity.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Moving away from EMR to a single self-managed EC2 instance destroys distributed processing capabilities and increases operational burden.

questions.question: An enterprise organization operates multiple AWS accounts managed through AWS Organizations. The finance team reports that Amazon EBS storage costs are rising rapidly, but it is difficult to identify which teams are generating unattached volumes and old snapshots. Which combination of features provides the most effective cost visibility and governance?

options.text: Use Amazon CloudWatch alarms on every EC2 instance to monitor local disk utilization and trigger cleanups.
Write a custom AWS Lambda script in each account to list EBS volumes and email a CSV report to the finance team daily.
Migrate all EBS volumes to Amazon EFS to automatically manage storage capacity.
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks across all accounts and set up AWS Cost Anomaly Detection with alerts sent to the finance team.

questions.explanation: AWS Trusted Advisor provides pre-built cost optimization checks (including unattached EBS volumes and old snapshots), and AWS Cost Anomaly Detection monitors spend patterns across AWS Organizations accounts.

wrongOptionNotes.A: CloudWatch alarms monitor instance-level metrics, but unattached EBS volumes and snapshots do not belong to running instances and will not be caught by instance metrics.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Writing and maintaining custom scripts across multiple accounts introduces unnecessary operational overhead when native AWS tools already provide this functionality.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Amazon EFS is a file storage service and is often more expensive than EBS block storage; migrating does not solve the root cause of unmanaged unattached volumes.

questions.question: A media streaming company stores terabytes of video content in Amazon S3. Viewers request videos globally. Data transfer out (DTO) costs from Amazon S3 to the internet are impacting the monthly budget significantly. What is the most cost-effective architecture to reduce data transfer costs?

options.text: Replicate the S3 bucket to every AWS Region globally using S3 Cross-Region Replication.
Deploy Amazon CloudFront in front of the S3 bucket to cache video content at edge locations globally.
Compress all video files using AWS Lambda before users download them.
Attach an Elastic Load Balancer in front of the S3 bucket to distribute client download requests.

questions.explanation: Using a Content Delivery Network like Amazon CloudFront caches static media content closer to users, lowering origin retrieval and reducing S3 internet data transfer out costs.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Replicating petabytes of video data across all global AWS regions incurs massive storage and replication data transfer costs, which would likely exceed the savings.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Video files (such as MP4 or MKV) are typically already compressed; attempting on-the-fly compression via Lambda for large files is computationally expensive and hits execution limits.
wrongOptionNotes.D: An Elastic Load Balancer cannot sit directly in front of S3 for public internet downloads in a way that reduces S3 data transfer costs, and ALBs incur their own hourly and data processing fees.

questions.question: A financial services firm runs a mission-critical transactional database on Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The database runs 24/7, and capacity requirements are stable and well-understood. The company wants to minimize the cost of this database workload over a 3-year period.

options.text: Configure Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 and let it scale down to zero capacity units during quiet hours.
Convert the database to run on Amazon EC2 Spot Instances managed by an Auto Scaling group.
Purchase 3-year Amazon RDS Reserved Instances with All Upfront payment for the Aurora database instances.
Rely entirely on AWS Free Tier eligibility for the database instances.

questions.explanation: When database capacity requirements are steady and predictable over a multi-year horizon, RDS/Aurora Reserved Instances offer the greatest cost savings over On-Demand pricing.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Aurora Serverless v2 does not scale down to zero; it maintains a minimum capacity (usually 0.5 ACUs) to keep the database warm and ready for connections.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Mission-critical relational databases require high availability and persistence; Spot Instances can be interrupted with a two-minute warning, making them unsuitable for primary databases.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Production enterprise database workloads far exceed the limits and duration of the AWS Free Tier.

questions.question: A company hosts a web application on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The database is hosted on Amazon RDS MySQL. Application usage analytics reveal that 90% of database queries are repetitive read requests for product catalog data that rarely changes. Database CPU utilization is high during peak hours.

options.text: Upgrade the RDS database instance to the largest available instance size.
Migrate the database storage from General Purpose SSD (gp2) to Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2).
Scale out the application EC2 instances using an Auto Scaling group.
Implement Amazon ElastiCache for Redis between the application and the RDS database to cache frequent read queries.

questions.explanation: Implementing a caching layer using Amazon ElastiCache offloads repetitive read queries from the relational database, optimizing both cost and performance.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Vertical scaling is an expensive brute-force approach that does not address the inefficiency of repeatedly querying the database for unchanging data.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Provisioned IOPS improves disk I/O performance, but the bottleneck is CPU utilization from repetitive query execution, which storage types alone will not resolve cost-effectively.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Adding more web servers increases the number of concurrent connections to the database, exacerbating the database CPU bottleneck rather than alleviating it.

questions.question: An analytics team runs transient data transformation jobs using Amazon EMR. The jobs take between 30 minutes and 2 hours to complete and are triggered via automated workflows. Currently, developers forget to terminate EMR clusters after jobs complete, resulting in significant waste.

options.text: Migrate the workload to Amazon EC2 instances running 24/7 with cron-based shutdown scripts.
Enable AWS Budgets to email developers whenever a cluster runs for more than 1 hour.
Configure automatic cluster termination by setting an idle timeout or using step concurrency limits so EMR terminates when steps complete.
Purchase 1-year Reserved Instances for the EMR core nodes.

questions.explanation: Transient workloads should leverage automated lifecycle features like EMR step completion termination to prevent charges accumulating from idle resources.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Managing standalone EC2 clusters manually increases operational overhead compared to native EMR automated step execution and auto-termination.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Sending emails relies on human intervention to manually terminate clusters, whereas native automated termination prevents waste proactively.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Reserved Instances are a poor choice for transient clusters that should be shut down when not in use, as you would pay for hours when the cluster does not even exist.

questions.question: A startup stores application logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. The logs are queried frequently for the first 7 days for troubleshooting, but after 7 days, they are rarely accessed. However, compliance regulations require retaining all logs for 3 years. The current logging costs are unsustainable.

options.text: Export the logs to Amazon S3 after 7 days and configure an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition them to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
Keep all logs in CloudWatch Logs and purchase CloudWatch Provisioned Concurrency.
Delete all log files after 7 days to eliminate storage costs entirely.
Store all logs on Amazon EBS volumes attached to a dedicated logging EC2 instance.

questions.explanation: Amazon CloudWatch Logs is optimized for active log analysis. For long-term compliance archiving, moving logs to Amazon S3 and transitioning them to S3 Glacier significantly reduces storage costs.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Provisioned Concurrency applies to AWS Lambda, not CloudWatch Logs, and CloudWatch storage pricing remains high regardless.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Deleting logs violates the 3-year compliance retention mandate.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Managing self-hosted logging servers on EBS increases operational burden, and EBS storage is more expensive than S3 Glacier for long-term retention.

questions.question: A multinational enterprise has hundreds of AWS accounts managed under AWS Organizations. The central cloud team needs a comprehensive mechanism to track spending trends, allocate costs by department using tags, and identify potential cost optimization opportunities across all accounts automatically.

options.text: Log into every AWS account individually each week and download the AWS Billing PDF invoice.
Enable AWS Cost Explorer, configure AWS Cost Allocation Tags, and set up AWS Trusted Advisor organizational recommendations.
Write a custom AWS Glue ETL job to parse CloudTrail logs and insert spending data into Amazon Redshift.
Attach Amazon CloudWatch billing alarms to the root user of every member account.

questions.explanation: AWS Cost Explorer combined with Cost Allocation Tags and AWS Trusted Advisor provides centralized, multi-account cost visibility and optimization recommendations.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual review of hundreds of individual accounts is operationally impossible and lacks granular tag-based attribution.
wrongOptionNotes.C: CloudTrail tracks API activity, not billing data. AWS provides native cost management tools that eliminate the need for complex custom data pipelines.
wrongOptionNotes.D: CloudWatch billing alarms alert on spending thresholds but do not provide detailed cost allocation reporting or optimization recommendations.

questions.question: An image-processing application runs on Amazon EC2 instances and downloads raw images from an Amazon S3 bucket in the same AWS Region, processes them, and uploads the results back to S3. Network data transfer costs between EC2 and S3 are higher than expected.

options.text: Ensure that a Gateway VPC Endpoint for Amazon S3 is configured in the VPC so traffic routes internally without traversing the public internet.
Enable AWS Transit Gateway between the EC2 VPC and the S3 bucket.
Deploy a NAT Gateway in every Availability Zone to route S3 traffic securely.
Migrate the application to run on physical on-premises servers connected via AWS Direct Connect.

questions.explanation: Using a Gateway VPC Endpoint for Amazon S3 allows EC2 instances within a VPC to access S3 buckets securely and cost-effectively without incurring NAT or public data transfer fees.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Amazon S3 does not attach to a Transit Gateway using VPC attachments; Gateway VPC Endpoints are the correct native mechanism for S3.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Routing S3 traffic through a NAT Gateway incurs hourly charges and data processing fees per GB, which increases network costs rather than optimizing them.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Direct Connect introduces data transfer out fees from AWS to on-premises and increases architectural complexity for a cloud-native workflow.

questions.question: A media company runs a frequently accessed web application backed by Amazon EBS storage. Over time, administrators have created numerous manual and automated snapshots of EBS volumes. Many snapshots are obsolete, but identifying which ones are associated with active volumes is challenging. Which approach provides automated cost optimization for EBS snapshots?

options.text: Write a bash script executed via cron on every EC2 instance to delete local snapshot files.
Detach all EBS volumes from EC2 instances when snapshots are taken.
Convert all EBS snapshots into Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) and store them in Glacier.
Implement Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) to automate snapshot creation, retention, and deletion policies.

questions.explanation: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM) provides a native, automated way to manage EBS snapshot lifecycles, reducing storage costs by deleting outdated snapshots.

wrongOptionNotes.A: EBS snapshots are stored in Amazon S3, not locally on EC2 instances; local cron scripts cannot manage EBS snapshots.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Detaching active production volumes to take snapshots causes application downtime and does not clean up obsolete snapshot history.
wrongOptionNotes.C: AMIs depend on snapshots; converting snapshots to AMIs does not delete old data and increases management complexity.

questions.question: A company is migrating a legacy .NET application to AWS. The application runs as a background Windows service that processes queue messages from Amazon SQS. The workload is sporadic, running intensely for 10 minutes every few hours. The company wants the most cost-optimized and serverless architecture.

options.text: Configure AWS Lambda to poll the SQS queue and execute the application code upon message arrival.
Provision a cluster of Windows Server EC2 instances running 24/7 with an Auto Scaling group.
Use Amazon RDS to host the SQS queue and trigger stored procedures.
Deploy the Windows service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate using a minimum of 2 tasks running continuously.

questions.explanation: For sporadic, event-driven workloads triggered by queues like SQS, AWS Lambda provides true pay-as-you-go pricing with zero idle cost.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Running Windows EC2 instances 24/7 incurs continuous hourly compute and Windows Server licensing costs, which is highly inefficient for a workload running only 10 minutes every few hours.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Amazon RDS is a relational database service, not a queue polling mechanism, and running an RDS instance 24/7 for this use case is cost-prohibitive.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Fargate tasks running continuously 24/7 cost significantly more than an event-driven AWS Lambda function for sporadic message processing.

questions.question: An analytics enterprise stores 500 TB of raw data in Amazon S3. The data is rarely accessed (less than once a quarter), but when queries run, users require retrieval within minutes. Budget constraints require minimizing storage costs as much as possible without sacrificing the quick retrieval requirement.

options.text: Store the data on Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS SSD (io2) volumes.
Transition the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
Keep all data in Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA).
Transition the data to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval provides an optimal balance between ultra-low storage costs and rapid retrieval times (minutes to hours) for infrequently accessed data.

wrongOptionNotes.A: EBS block storage is designed for active database and OS disks, costing orders of magnitude more than S3 for 500 TB of archival data.
wrongOptionNotes.C: S3 Standard-IA storage costs are significantly higher than S3 Glacier storage tiers, making it less cost-effective for data accessed less than once a quarter.
wrongOptionNotes.D: S3 Glacier Deep Archive has the lowest storage cost, but retrieval times take between 2 to 12 hours, which fails the user requirement of retrieval within minutes.

questions.question: An e-commerce enterprise runs a catalog service on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The traffic fluctuates predictably, peaking during the midday hours and dropping significantly at night. Management requires a cost-optimized compute solution that automatically scales down the fleet overnight while ensuring compute capacity is immediately available during peak hours without performance degradation.

options.text: Configure an Auto Scaling group with Target Tracking scaling policies and Scheduled Scaling actions to adjust minimum capacity ahead of known peak hours.
Maintain a static fleet of On-Demand Instances sized for peak load to guarantee high availability and eliminate scaling complexity.
Migrate the application entirely to AWS Lambda to eliminate idle compute costs during nighttime hours.
Purchase All Upfront Reserved Instances matching the peak capacity requirements and use EC2 Auto Scaling only for failover purposes.

questions.explanation: Combining Auto Scaling with Scheduled Scaling and Target Tracking policies provides the optimal balance of cost savings and performance by matching capacity to predictable load patterns.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Maintaining a static fleet sized for peak load during nighttime hours results in significant unnecessary spend, violating cost-optimization principles.
wrongOptionNotes.C: Rewriting a legacy EC2-based catalog service to serverless AWS Lambda requires significant development effort and might introduce cold start latency that impacts user experience during traffic peaks.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Purchasing Reserved Instances for peak capacity means paying for idle instances during off-peak hours, failing to optimize costs through scaling.

questions.question: A financial services firm runs a relational database on Amazon RDS for MySQL. The database experiences heavy read traffic during business hours and minimal activity at night. To optimize operational costs without impacting application performance, a solutions architect must recommend a strategy for the database tier.

options.text: Migrate the database to Amazon DynamoDB to take advantage of on-demand capacity billing.
Convert the database instance to use Amazon EBS provisioned IOPS storage with autoscaling storage enabled.
Scale down the Amazon RDS instance class during off-peak hours and scale it back up prior to business hours.
Provision Amazon RDS Read Replicas and route read traffic away from the primary database instance, stopping the replicas during off-peak hours.

questions.explanation: Scaling down RDS instance classes during idle periods directly minimizes hourly compute expenditure, which is a common pattern for databases with strict business-hour usage windows.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Migrating a relational database to NoSQL involves major application rewrites and schema redesign, making it impractical purely for operational cost reduction.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Provisioned IOPS is more expensive and adjusting storage size or IOPS does not reduce the compute costs associated with the idle database engine.
wrongOptionNotes.D: RDS Read Replicas cannot be stopped independently while keeping the primary active in a way that preserves replication topologies seamlessly without recreation.

questions.question: A global news agency stores a massive archive of high-resolution images in Amazon S3. Content editors frequently access images created within the last 30 days, occasionally access images up to 90 days old, and rarely access files older than 90 days. The finance team mandates a reduction in S3 storage costs.

options.text: Delete all image files older than 30 days to permanently eliminate storage costs.
Transition all S3 objects immediately upon upload to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval and configure lifecycle rules to delete them after 90 days.
Apply an S3 Lifecycle policy to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) after 30 days, and to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days.
Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering across the entire bucket without setting any lifecycle expiration or transition rules.

questions.explanation: Amazon S3 Lifecycle policies allow automated, cost-effective transitions of data to cooler storage tiers based on object age and access frequency.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Deleting business-critical historical assets violates data retention policies and business requirements.
wrongOptionNotes.B: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is not suitable for objects accessed frequently within the first 30 days due to retrieval fees and higher minimum storage duration charges.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between tiers, it incurs monitoring and automation fees that may be higher than explicit lifecycle rules for predictable access patterns.

questions.question: An analytics startup runs resource-intensive containerized batch jobs using Amazon ECS on Amazon EC2. The jobs can be interrupted at any time and rerun from the last checkpoint without data loss. The company wants to minimize compute costs as much as possible.

options.text: Configure an ECS cluster backed by an Auto Scaling group using Amazon EC2 Spot Instances with an appropriate capacity provider strategy.
Purchase Compute Savings Plans covering 100% of the projected steady-state usage while running standard On-Demand EC2 instances.
Run all ECS tasks exclusively on AWS Fargate Spot instances.
Provision a dedicated Amazon EMR cluster with reserved instances to process the containerized batch workloads.

questions.explanation: For fault-tolerant, interruptible workloads, leveraging Amazon EC2 Spot Instances via ECS capacity providers yields maximum cost savings.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Savings Plans offer good discounts, but Spot instances offer significantly higher discounts for interruptible batch workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While Fargate Spot reduces costs, managing underlying EC2 Spot instances provides even deeper discounts for fault-tolerant batch workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Using EMR for simple containerized batch jobs introduces unnecessary architectural complexity and higher baseline costs compared to ECS on EC2 Spot.

questions.question: A multinational corporation has multiple business units deploying resources across dozens of AWS accounts. The central cloud team notices significant wastage due to unattached Amazon EBS volumes and idle Elastic IP addresses left behind by terminated instances. The team needs a centralized, automated mechanism to identify and report these cost optimization opportunities.

options.text: Manually run AWS CLI scripts from the master account on a weekly basis to audit all regional EC2 instances and volumes.
Write custom AWS Lambda functions in each account to scan for unattached volumes and send an email alert to the finance team daily.
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor organizational view to continuously identify cost optimization recommendations, such as idle resources and unattached EBS volumes across all member accounts.
Configure Amazon CloudWatch billing alarms in each account to trigger whenever EBS storage costs exceed a static threshold.

questions.explanation: AWS Trusted Advisor organizational view provides centralized visibility into cost optimization opportunities like unattached EBS volumes and idle resources across all AWS accounts.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Manual auditing does not scale effectively across hundreds of accounts and introduces human error and operational toil.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Maintaining custom Lambda scripts across multiple accounts introduces operational overhead and redundant code compared to native AWS services.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Billing alarms alert you to overall cost increases after the fact, but they do not identify the specific idle resources causing the waste.

questions.question: An enterprise application stores unstructured logs and document exports in Amazon S3. The data volume is growing by 50 TB per month. Access to these files drops sharply after 14 days, and after 60 days, the files are almost never accessed, though compliance mandates retaining them for 7 years. The storage cost is currently unacceptably high.

options.text: Delete all files automatically after 60 days using an S3 Lifecycle expiration rule to avoid long-term storage fees.
Use S3 Lifecycle configuration to transition objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, and to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 60 days.
Compress all objects using gzip locally before uploading them, and keep them in the S3 Standard storage tier indefinitely.
Migrate all data to Amazon Elastic File System (EFS) Infrequent Access tier for automated cost savings.

questions.explanation: Transitioning infrequently accessed compliance data to S3 Glacier Deep Archive via S3 Lifecycle rules minimizes long-term storage expenses while satisfying retention policies.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Deleting the files violates the 7-year compliance retention mandate.
wrongOptionNotes.C: While compression helps, it does not solve the long-term cost issue as effectively as tiering cold data down to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Amazon EFS is designed for file storage attached to compute instances and is significantly more expensive than Amazon S3 for storing massive static object archives.

questions.question: A software development company runs a steady-state backend API on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The application runs 24/7 with a predictable, constant baseline load. The finance team wants to minimize the compute expenditure over a 3-year commitment period.

options.text: Purchase Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to cover the 24/7 steady-state baseline load.
Rely entirely on EC2 Auto Scaling with On-Demand instances to react dynamically to the steady-state traffic.
Purchase Compute Savings Plans with a 3-year All Upfront payment option to cover the steady-state baseline usage.
Deploy the backend API onto AWS Lambda functions with provisioned concurrency enabled.

questions.explanation: Compute Savings Plans offer flexible, deep discounts for steady-state workloads across EC2, Fargate, and Lambda when committed for a 3-year term.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Spot instances can be reclaimed by AWS with a 2-minute warning, making them unsuitable for mission-critical steady-state 24/7 baseline production workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.B: On-Demand instances without commitment discounts are the most expensive way to run predictable, steady-state workloads.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Provisioned concurrency on Lambda for a 24/7 steady-state workload often costs more than running optimized EC2 instances with Savings Plans.

questions.question: An enterprise data warehouse runs on Amazon Redshift, consisting of multiple dc2.large worker nodes. The cluster operates 24/7. Query volume remains stable throughout the year. The chief financial officer asks the solutions architect to reduce the Amazon Redshift operational costs.

options.text: Convert the Redshift cluster from dc2 nodes to ra3 nodes with managed storage without checking reservation options.
Pause the Redshift cluster every evening and resume it every morning using scheduled AWS Lambda functions.
Purchase Amazon Redshift Reserved Nodes for the existing cluster configuration with a 1-year or 3-year commitment.
Migrate all Redshift tables to Amazon DynamoDB to take advantage of provisioned throughput billing.

questions.explanation: For steady-state 24/7 Amazon Redshift clusters, purchasing Redshift Reserved Nodes is the most direct and effective cost-optimization strategy.

wrongOptionNotes.A: While ra3 nodes decouple compute and storage, reserved node purchases provide immediate and predictable cost reductions for fixed 24/7 clusters.
wrongOptionNotes.B: The scenario states the cluster operates 24/7 and query volume is steady, implying pausing it nightly would disrupt business operations.
wrongOptionNotes.D: DynamoDB is a NoSQL key-value store and is unsuited for complex analytical data warehouse queries.

questions.question: A company is designing a data ingestion pipeline where raw files are dropped into an Amazon S3 bucket. A Lambda function processes each file and writes results to an Amazon DynamoDB table. The arrival rate of files is highly sporadic, with hours of zero traffic followed by sudden surges of thousands of files per minute. The company wants to optimize costs for DynamoDB.

options.text: Implement DynamoDB auto scaling with a target utilization of 90% on Provisioned Capacity mode.
Migrate the DynamoDB table to Amazon Aurora Serverless v2 with minimum capacity set to zero.
Configure the DynamoDB table to use On-Demand capacity mode.
Provision a fixed capacity of 500 Read Capacity Units and 500 Write Capacity Units to handle the peak surges.

questions.explanation: DynamoDB On-Demand mode is ideal for unpredictable, spiky workloads because you pay only for the reads and writes your application actually performs, without manual capacity planning.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Auto scaling takes time to react to sudden, spiky traffic surges, which can result in request throttling (ThrottlingExceptions) before scaling completes.
wrongOptionNotes.B: Aurora Serverless v2 scales down to 0.5 ACUs, but does not scale to absolute zero, and relational databases add unnecessary overhead for simple key-value logging pipelines.
wrongOptionNotes.D: Provisioning fixed capacity for peak surges leads to massive over-provisioning and wasted spend during the frequent hours of zero traffic.

questions.question: A media company stores terabytes of raw video assets in an Amazon S3 bucket. Editors download these files infrequently across different global regions. Data transfer out (DTO) fees from Amazon S3 to the internet are driving up the monthly AWS bill significantly.

options.text: Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy all video assets to every AWS Region globally.
Move the video files to Amazon EBS General Purpose SSD (gp3) volumes attached to EC2 instances acting as file servers.
Deploy Amazon CloudFront in front of the Amazon S3 bucket to cache video assets at edge locations.
Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket to optimize upload speeds for viewers.

questions.explanation: Integrating Amazon CloudFront with Amazon S3 leverages AWS edge caching to lower data transfer costs and improve global content delivery efficiency.

wrongOptionNotes.A: Replicating terabytes of data across all global regions incurs massive storage replication costs that far outweigh any potential DTO savings.
wrongOptionNotes.B: EBS storage is substantially more expensive per gigabyte than S3 and does not solve global internet data transfer cost challenges.
wrongOptionNotes.D: S3 Transfer Acceleration optimizes data uploads into S3 via AWS Edge locations, but does not reduce data transfer out costs for downloads.

questions.question: A financial firm runs a nightly data processing job using Amazon EMR. The job takes exactly 4 hours to complete, running every night at midnight. The cluster uses On-Demand EC2 instances. Management wants to reduce the compute costs of this predictable, transient workload.

options.text: Configure the EMR cluster to use Amazon EC2 Spot Instances for the task and core nodes.
Keep the EMR cluster running 24/7 on Reserved Instances so it is always warm and ready for the midnight job.
Migrate the EMR cluster workloads to AWS Lambda functions with maximum execution timeout configured.
Purchase 3-year Compute Savings Plans to cover the nightly 4-hour EMR cluster execution.

questions.explanation: Transient analytics workloads on Amazon EMR should leverage Amazon EC2 Spot Instances to achieve maximum cost savings without risking permanent infrastructure waste.

wrongOptionNotes.B: Keeping an analytics cluster running 24/7 when it is only used for 4 hours a night wastes significant compute resources.
wrongOptionNotes.C: AWS Lambda has a maximum execution limit of 15 minutes, making it impossible to run a 4-hour data processing job natively.
wrongOptionNotes.D: While Savings Plans apply to EMR instances, purchasing a commitment for a workload that runs only 4 hours a day results in 20 hours of daily idle commitment waste.
